questions.q: What were the three separate contributing causes behind the case study's intermittent "Too many SOQL queries: 101" error?
options: A single typo in the OpportunityTrigger that was fixed by adding one missing semicolon

A per-record SOQL query inside the OpportunityTrigger loop, a Get Records element inside a Flow loop sharing the same transaction, and rising Opportunity volume making the existing anti-patterns cross the limit now
A corrupted debug log that misreported the actual query count
An expired Salesforce license that disabled half the org's automation
questions.explain: The case study deliberately combines a trigger-level anti-pattern, a Flow-level anti-pattern sharing the same transaction, and a scalability trend making both worse over time — exactly the kind of multi-cause bug real performance work often involves.

questions.q: Why would fixing only the OpportunityTrigger, and leaving the Flow's Get Records element inside its loop untouched, likely have left the bug only partially resolved?
options: Because Flow automation runs in a completely separate transaction from Apex, so fixing the trigger alone would have fully solved it
Because Flows cannot cause governor limit exceptions under any circumstances

Because Flow and Apex share the same transaction and the same cumulative governor limit budget, so the Flow's per-iteration queries would still be adding to the same total that caused the original exception
Because the Flow's queries don't count toward any governor limit at all
questions.explain: Since Flow and Apex share one transaction's cumulative limit budget (per Lesson 5), leaving the Flow's loop-based querying in place would still contribute to the same total, even after the trigger itself was fixed.

questions.q: What did the symptom pattern — "only on large deals," "getting worse over time" — suggest before any code was even read?
options: Nothing meaningful; symptom patterns are not useful evidence until code has been reviewed
That the issue was caused entirely by a platform-wide Salesforce outage
That the fix must involve purchasing additional storage, unrelated to code

"Only large deals" pointed toward a cost that scales with related-record count (a per-record loop), and "getting worse over time" pointed toward a scalability trend crossing a limit that used to have headroom
questions.explain: A per-record loop's cost scales with how many related records exist, matching "only large deals," and a scalability trend (Lesson 6) explains why a previously-tolerable anti-pattern starts failing as data volume grows — both are diagnostic clues before reading any code.

questions.q: In the bulkified OpportunityTrigger fix, what data structure is built to avoid querying Contacts once per Opportunity?
options: A Map<Id, List<Contact>> keyed by AccountId, built from one query against the full set of collected AccountIds
A separate Queueable job that runs once per Opportunity
A nested for loop that still queries once per Opportunity, just written differently
A static variable that caches the first Opportunity's Contacts for reuse on all others
questions.explain: The fix collects all relevant AccountIds into a Set, queries Contacts once for that whole set, and organizes the results into a Map keyed by AccountId so each Opportunity's related Contacts can be looked up without any additional query.

questions.q: Why does the case study insist on re-measuring with a fresh debug log after applying both fixes, rather than assuming they worked?
options: Because Salesforce requires a debug log to be attached to every deployment by policy

Because confirming a fix with real evidence (a fresh CUMULATIVE_LIMIT_USAGE reading) follows the same evidence-based discipline as reproducing the original problem, rather than assuming success without verification
Because re-measurement is only necessary when the first fix attempt fails
Because debug logs automatically revert code changes that don't improve performance
questions.explain: The same evidence-based discipline that applied to reproducing the problem (Lesson 10, step 1) applies to confirming the fix — re-measuring with real data rather than assuming the fix worked closes the loop properly.
